title: The King's Table
subtitle: Daniel 1
description: Four exiles at the king's table refuse the royal food, and a ten-day test begins a career that outlasts Babylon.
paragraphs: Daniel's book opens before Jerusalem falls, in the first taking of the city. “In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it.” The Lord delivered the king and some of the temple articles into his hand, and the articles went to the house of his god in Shinar. Then the king turned his attention to people. Ashpenaz, chief of the court officials, was ordered to bring in Israelite youths from the royal family and the nobility, “young men without blemish, handsome, gifted in all wisdom, knowledgeable, quick to understand, and qualified to serve in the king’s palace,” and to teach them “the language and literature of the Chaldeans.” The program ran three years, and it ran on the king's own food and wine.

Among the youths taken were four from Judah whose names the book gives before anything else about them: “Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.” The chief official renamed them, as conquerors rename the things they have taken: Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego. The names were the program in miniature, new identities for a new service. It is at the table, not at the naming, that the first resistance comes. “But Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine. So he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself.” The text says God had already gone ahead of the request: He “had granted Daniel favor and compassion from the chief official,” and the official liked him and was still afraid.

The fear was reasonable. The king had assigned the food himself, and a steward whose charges thinned on vegetables would answer with his head: “You would endanger my head before the king!” So Daniel took the request down a level, to the steward set over the four of them, and made it an experiment instead of a defiance. “Please test your servants for ten days. Let us be given only vegetables to eat and water to drink. Then compare our appearances with those of the young men who are eating the royal food, and deal with your servants according to what you see.” Ten days, a visible result, and the decision left in the steward's hands. It is the first display in the book of the quality that will keep Daniel alive in three courts: he does not bend, and he does not bluster.

At the end of ten days the four “looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who were eating the king’s food”, and the steward quietly kept the arrangement for the remaining three years, withholding the royal portions and bringing vegetables instead. What the training was supposed to produce, God gave directly: “To these four young men God gave knowledge and understanding in every kind of literature and wisdom. And Daniel had insight into all kinds of visions and dreams.” The last clause is planted like a seed. Insight into visions and dreams is named as a gift before any king has dreamed anything, and the rest of the book grows out of it.

When the three years ended and the class was presented, the king examined them himself and “found no one equal to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,” and in every matter he consulted, “he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom.” So the four exiles entered the service of the king who had carried them off. The chapter's last line then does something the reader should not rush past: it measures Daniel's whole career in advance. “And Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus.” Cyrus is the Persian who will conquer Babylon itself. The boy who would not defile himself at the king's table will still be standing when the king's empire is gone, and the book that follows is the record of how.

title: Tell Me the Dream
subtitle: Daniel 2
description: Nebuchadnezzar demands the dream itself, the wise men fail, and Daniel's night prayer stops an execution.
paragraphs: In the second year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams that troubled his spirit until sleep left him, and he summoned his magicians, enchanters, sorcerers, and astrologers to explain them. What he demanded was beyond interpretation. He would not tell them the dream; they were to tell him, both the dream and what it meant. “My word is final: If you do not tell me the dream and its interpretation, you will be cut into pieces and your houses will be reduced to rubble.” The astrologers asked twice for the dream itself and were accused of stalling, and at last they said the thing their whole profession existed to avoid saying: “No one on earth can do what the king requests!” and “What the king requests is so difficult that no one can tell it to him except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals.” The text pauses on a fact about its own language at exactly this point: the astrologers answered the king in Aramaic (2:4), and from here through chapter 7 the book runs in Aramaic, the language of the empire, rather than Hebrew.

The king's fury turned the failed consultation into a general execution: the decree went out to destroy all the wise men of Babylon, and Daniel and his friends were on the list with the rest. When Arioch, the king's guard commander, came for them, “Daniel responded with discretion and tact” and asked the question that bought the book its hinge: “Why is the decree from the king so harsh?” Arioch explained, and Daniel went straight to the king and asked for time, promising the interpretation. A condemned man requested an audience, and the king who had ordered the executions granted the condemned man time.

Daniel went home and laid the matter before Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, “urging them to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his friends would not be killed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.” The four who had once asked a steward for ten days now asked heaven for one night, and in the night “the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision”. His first act with the answer was not to run to the palace. He blessed the God of heaven: “Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, for wisdom and power belong to Him. He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them.”

The hymn runs on through the deep structure of things: “He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him.” Then it lands on the night's specific mercy: “To You, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, because You have given me wisdom and power. And now You have made known to me what we have requested, for You have made known to us the dream of the king.” Only then did Daniel go to Arioch with the order stopped: “Do not execute the wise men of Babylon! Bring me before the king, and I will give him the interpretation.”

Arioch hurried him in and took the credit available, announcing a man found “among the exiles from Judah,” and the king put the question plainly: could Daniel tell what he had seen, as well as its meaning? Daniel's answer begins by agreeing with the astrologers completely. “No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires. But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days.” And he closed off the last misunderstanding before it could form: the mystery had been revealed to him “not because I have more wisdom than any man alive, but in order that the interpretation might be made known to the king.” Then the condemned exile began to tell the king of Babylon his own dream back to him.

title: The Statue and the Stone
subtitle: Daniel 2
description: A statue of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, a stone cut without hands, and the kingdom that will never be destroyed.
paragraphs: The dream was a statue, and Daniel described it as the king had seen it: “a great statue appeared. A great and dazzling statue stood before you, and its form was awesome.” Its head was pure gold, its chest and arms silver, its belly and thighs bronze, its legs iron, “and its feet were part iron and part clay.” The materials run downhill in value as the eye descends, gold to clay, while the strength runs the other way at the middle, silver giving way to bronze and iron before the strange, mixed feet. It stood there enormous and gleaming, a single figure made of five substances and four kingdoms, though the king did not know that yet.

Then the dream moved. “As you watched, a stone was cut out, but not by human hands. It struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them.” The whole figure came down at once, “the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold were shattered and became like chaff on the threshing floor in summer. The wind carried them away, and not a trace of them could be found.” And the stone did the opposite of disappearing: “the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.” The dream ended there, on a mountain where an empire had been.

Daniel turned to the interpretation without flinching, and its first word was personal. “You, O king, are the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given sovereignty, power, strength, and glory.” The head of gold is identified outright, the only part of the statue the chapter names: “You are that head of gold.” Nebuchadnezzar's empire is a gift held from heaven, and the dream that terrified him is mostly about what comes after him. “But after you, there will arise another kingdom, inferior to yours. Next, a third kingdom, one of bronze, will rule the whole earth. Finally, there will be a fourth kingdom as strong as iron; for iron shatters and crushes all things.” The text names none of the successors. It gives the king metals, sequence, and character, and leaves the names to history.

The feet get the closest reading. The kingdom there will be divided, iron's strength mixed with clay's brittleness, and “the peoples will mix with one another but will not hold together any more than iron mixes with clay.” Then the interpretation reaches the stone: “In the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people. It will shatter all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but will itself stand forever.” The stone cut without hands and the kingdom set up by God are the same event seen from two sides, and Daniel ends where the astrologers could not begin: “The dream is true, and its interpretation is trustworthy.”

The king who had ordered every wise man in Babylon cut to pieces now fell on his face before one of them, and paid Daniel homage, and ordered offerings and incense presented to him. His confession was exact about where the power lay: “Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery.” Daniel was promoted, loaded with gifts, made “ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon,” the same wise men whose lives his prayer had saved that morning. And his first recorded act in office was for the other three: “at Daniel’s request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon, while Daniel remained in the king’s court.” The four who had eaten vegetables together now ran Babylon together.

title: The Image of Gold and the Furnace
subtitle: Daniel 3
description: A golden image ninety feet high, three men who will not bow, and a fourth figure walking in the furnace.
paragraphs: The next thing Nebuchadnezzar built was bigger than the statue in his dream and made of one metal all the way down. “King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue sixty cubits high and six cubits wide, and he set it up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.” Ninety feet of gold on an open plain, and every official of the empire summoned to its dedication: satraps, prefects, governors, advisers, treasurers, judges, magistrates. The herald's command was set to music. When the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, and pipes sounded, every knee in the empire was to go down, and “whoever does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace.” Daniel is never mentioned in this chapter. The book leaves him out of it entirely and gives the stand to his three friends, under the names Babylon gave them.

Some astrologers came forward and accused the Jews by name: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, the king's own appointees over Babylon's province, “have refused to serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.” Nebuchadnezzar, furious, still offered them the music once more and a second chance to fall, and ended with the question the chapter exists to answer: “Then what god will be able to deliver you from my hands?” The three answered together, and their answer is the calmest speech in the book. “O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king. But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.”

The king's face changed, and he ordered the furnace heated “seven times hotter than usual,” and his mightiest soldiers bound the three, still in their robes, trousers, and turbans, and threw them in. The king's command was so urgent and the fire so hot that “the fiery flames killed the men who carried up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.” The executioners died at the furnace door and the condemned fell in bound. Then the king, watching, jumped up in amazement and asked his advisers whether they had not thrown three bound men into the fire. “Look!” he exclaimed. “I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire,” “and the fourth looks like a son of the gods!”

Nebuchadnezzar came as close to the door as the heat allowed and called them out himself: “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out!” They came out in front of the whole assembled government, and the officials saw what the text reports like an inventory: “the fire had no effect on the bodies of these men. Not a hair of their heads was singed, their robes were unaffected, and there was no smell of fire on them.” The fire had burned exactly one thing, the ropes. The king who had asked what god could deliver from his hands now answered his own question in a blessing: “Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him.”

He followed the blessing with a decree protecting their God across the empire, on pain of the same sentence he had once pronounced on his wise men: “For there is no other god who can deliver in this way.” And the three who would not bow were promoted in the province of Babylon. The chapter leaves the empire's arithmetic standing for the reader: the music had demanded every knee, and the only men left upright at the end were the ones who had refused to kneel, while the king who built the image spent the chapter's close praising the God who had walked His servants through the king's own fire.

title: The King's Letter: A Tree in the Midst of the Land
subtitle: Daniel 4
description: Nebuchadnezzar's own letter tells of a great tree, a watcher, and a stump left banded in the ground.
paragraphs: Chapter 4 arrives as a document, the only one of its kind in the book: a letter from the king of Babylon to the whole earth. “King Nebuchadnezzar, To the people of every nation and language who dwell in all the earth: May your prosperity be multiplied.” What the letter announces is not a victory or a decree but “the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for me,” and it opens with a confession no Babylonian liturgy contained: “How great are His signs, how mighty His wonders! His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; His dominion endures from generation to generation.” The king writing is the king from the far side of the story, telling it backward, and the letter never pretends otherwise.

Inside the letter, the earlier king is at ease and flourishing in his palace when a dream frightens him, and once again the wise men of Babylon fail, and once again Daniel comes in last. The king explains why he trusts this exile above his own guild: Daniel is the one “in whom is the spirit of the holy gods,” and no mystery baffles him. The dream he tells is of a tree. “There was a tree in the midst of the land, and its height was great.” It grew until its top reached the sky and it was visible to the ends of the earth, beautiful in leaf, heavy with fruit, “and upon it was food for all,” shelter for the beasts below and nests for the birds above, every creature fed from one trunk.

Then a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven and gave the order against it: “Cut down the tree and chop off its branches; strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit.” The stump was to be left, banded with iron and bronze in the grass, and the decree changed pronouns mid-sentence, tree to man: “Let him be drenched with the dew of heaven and graze with the beasts on the grass of the earth. Let his mind be changed from that of a man, and let him be given the mind of a beast till seven times pass him by.” The watcher stated the decree's purpose out loud, so the whole earth would know what the tree was for: “so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes, setting over it the lowliest of men.”

Daniel heard the dream and was perplexed and alarmed for a time, silent before the king he served, until the king himself told him not to fear it. His wish is the wish of a loyal counselor who has to deliver the worst news in the empire: “may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies!” Then he said it: “you, O king, are that tree! For you have become great and strong; your greatness has grown to reach the sky, and your dominion extends to the ends of the earth.” The cutting is the king's exile from mankind: driven out to live with the beasts, eating grass like an ox, drenched with heaven's dew, “until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes.”

But the stump was left in the ground on purpose, banded, not burned, and Daniel read that detail as the dream's mercy: “your kingdom will be restored to you as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules.” What Daniel did next no other courtier in the book attempts. He counseled the king against the decree, as if a sentence from heaven might still be answered by repentance on earth: “Therefore, may my advice be pleasing to you, O king. Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed. Perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity.” The letter pauses there, on the perhaps. The king has been warned by his God, interpreted by his exile, and counseled like a friend, and the letter's next line is a date: all this happened to King Nebuchadnezzar.

title: Until You Acknowledge That Heaven Rules
subtitle: Daniel 4
description: Twelve months of warning run out on a palace roof, and the king goes out to pasture until he looks up.
paragraphs: Twelve months went by. Whatever Nebuchadnezzar made of Daniel's counsel, the letter he later wrote records no reformation, only the interval, and then the king walking on the roof of his palace in Babylon at the height of it all. The sentence that undid him was spoken to no one in particular, a man admiring his own reflection in a city: “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” Every clause in it steps around the dream. Not given, built. Not by the Most High who rules the kingdom of mankind, by my power. Not for the living to know who rules, for the glory of my majesty.

The voice answered while the words were still in his mouth. “It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, that the kingdom has departed from you.” The terms were the dream's terms, word for word: driven from mankind, dwelling with the beasts of the field, eating grass like an ox, seven times passing by, “until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes.” No invasion, no usurper, no assassination. The mightiest king on earth was not overthrown. He was sent out to pasture, and the throne stood empty behind him with the empire still running, waiting to see whether anyone would come back to it.

“At that moment the sentence against Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled. He was driven away from mankind. He ate grass like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew like the feathers of an eagle and his nails like the claws of a bird.” The letter does not say who governed Babylon in those years, or how long seven times lasted, or who fed him. It is interested in one thing only, the acknowledgment the decree was built to produce, and it withholds the scene of it until the king's own grammar changes: from he to I.

“But at the end of those days I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me.” The first act of the restored mind was praise, and the letter gives the hymn in full: “For His dominion is an everlasting dominion, and His kingdom endures from generation to generation. All the peoples of the earth are counted as nothing, and He does as He pleases with the army of heaven and the peoples of the earth. There is no one who can restrain His hand or say to Him, ‘What have You done?’” This is the head of gold of Daniel's interpretation, the king to whom God gave sovereignty, power, strength, and glory, saying at last what the gift had always meant: the peoples are counted as nothing, his own throne included.

With the sanity came everything back: honor, splendor, counselors and nobles seeking him out, the throne restored and “surpassing greatness was added to me.” The letter closes on the doxology that explains why a king would publish his own humiliation to every nation and language on earth: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven, for all His works are true and all His ways are just. And He is able to humble those who walk in pride.” Babylon's archive kept no such letter. Daniel's book did, and it stands in the record as the testimony of the empire's greatest king that the kingdom of mankind was never his.

title: The Writing on the Wall
subtitle: Daniel 5
description: Temple vessels at a feast, a hand writing on the wall, and a kingdom weighed and divided in one night.
paragraphs: A generation has passed since the king's letter. Nebuchadnezzar is gone, and Belshazzar, whom the book calls his son, holds “a great feast for a thousand of his nobles” in a Babylon that has new enemies outside its walls. Under the influence of the wine, Belshazzar ordered a sacrilege as entertainment: the gold and silver vessels “that Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken from the temple in Jerusalem” were brought in, and the king drank from them with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines. As they drank, “they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone.” The temple cups went around a room toasting the very metals Daniel's statue had taught Babylon to outgrow, and the feast reached the moment the book was written to preserve.

“At that moment the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall, near the lampstand in the royal palace.” No arm, no body, only fingers, writing where the lamplight fell. The king watched the hand, “his face grew pale and his thoughts so alarmed him that his hips gave way and his knees knocked together.” The wise men came in and failed completely; they “could not read the inscription or interpret it for him,” and the king's terror only deepened.

It was the queen who remembered what the court had forgotten. “There is a man in your kingdom who has the spirit of the holy gods in him,” she said, an old man from the old reign, chief of the magicians under Nebuchadnezzar, a solver of riddles named Daniel.

Daniel was brought in and offered the standard fee, purple, a gold chain, and the third place in the kingdom, and he refused the fee before he read a word: “You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else. Nevertheless, I will read the inscription for the king and interpret it for him.” Then, before the interpretation, he preached the history Belshazzar had grown up on and learned nothing from. “the Most High God gave your father Nebuchadnezzar sovereignty and greatness, glory and honor”, and when his heart hardened with pride he was deposed and driven out to eat grass “until he acknowledged that the Most High God rules over the kingdom of mankind.” The sermon turned on one sentence: “But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this.” Instead he had lifted himself against the Lord of heaven with the temple vessels in his hands, and “failed to glorify the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways.”

“Now this is the inscription that was written: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN.” Daniel read the words as a set of scales. “MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end. TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient. PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.” Belshazzar kept his bargain anyway and had Daniel robed in purple and proclaimed third in a kingdom that had hours left. “That very night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was slain, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.” The vessels went back out of the banquet hall into history, and Daniel, near eighty by the book's own arithmetic, remained: the third empire of his life was arriving before morning.

title: The Lions' Den
subtitle: Daniel 6
description: A decree Daniel cannot obey, an upper room with open windows, and a king who spends the night fasting.
paragraphs: The new empire reorganized at once: Darius appointed 120 satraps over the kingdom and three administrators over them, “including Daniel,” to keep the king from loss. Daniel's extraordinary spirit distinguished him so quickly that the king “planned to set him over the whole kingdom,” and the plan made him a target. The other administrators and satraps audited him for a charge concerning the kingdom and found the audit useless, “because he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him.” Their conclusion is the chapter's backhanded tribute: “We will never find any charge against this Daniel unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.” The only exploitable fact about Daniel was his religion, so they built the trap out of it.

The instrument was flattery aimed at the throne. All the administrators, they told Darius, had agreed on a decree: for thirty days, anyone who petitions any god or man except the king would be thrown into the den of lions, and the document was to be signed under the law of the Medes and Persians, “which cannot be repealed.” Darius signed. Daniel's response is told without drama, and the absence of drama is the point. “Now when Daniel learned that the document had been signed, he went into his house, where the windows of his upper room opened toward Jerusalem, and three times a day he got down on his knees, prayed, and gave thanks to his God, just as he had done before.” He did not hide the prayers, change the hour, or lower a blind. The men who set the trap found him at it as a group, exactly where his whole career said he would be.

The law they had designed for Daniel caught the king instead. Darius, told that Daniel “still makes his petition three times a day,” was “deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel, and he labored until sundown to rescue him,” and found no lever in his own empire strong enough to move the decree he had signed. At sundown he gave the order himself, and his words at the den's mouth were a confession disguised as a hope: “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!” A stone was laid over the opening and sealed with the king's signet and his nobles' rings, so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed by anyone, including the king.

The palace kept the vigil the den did not need. Darius “spent the night fasting. No entertainment was brought before him, and sleep fled from him,” and at first light he hurried to the den and cried out “in a voice of anguish,” asking whether Daniel's God, whom he served continually, had been able to deliver him from the lions. The answer came up out of the sealed pit in the court formula, intact: “O king, may you live forever! My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, for I was found innocent in His sight, and I have done no wrong against you, O king.” Daniel was lifted out, and “no wounds whatsoever were found on him, because he had trusted in his God.”

The men who had accused him were thrown in with their children and wives, and the lions overpowered them before they reached the bottom. Then Darius wrote his own addition to the book's growing archive of royal testimony, a decree to every nation and language in his kingdom to tremble before Daniel's God: “For He is the living God, and He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end. He delivers and rescues; He performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth, for He has rescued Daniel from the power of the lions.” The court stories close with the career summary the first chapter promised: “So Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.” Three empires have now had their say about Daniel's God. The rest of the book is Daniel's own record of what he was shown.

title: Four Beasts from the Sea
subtitle: Daniel 7
description: Daniel dreams now: four beasts from the sea, a court of fire, and One like the Son of Man given forever.
paragraphs: The book's second half opens with a date that reaches backward. “In the first year of the reign of Belshazzar over Babylon, Daniel had a dream, and visions passed through his mind as he lay on his bed.” The feast of chapter 5 has not happened yet in the book's own order, and the fall of Babylon is still years away, but the dream comes to Daniel in his own room now, not to a king on a throne, and for the first time the prophet is the dreamer instead of the interpreter. “He wrote down the dream,” the text says, and what follows is his own summary of his own account, signed in the first person: I, Daniel, looked, and I saw.

“In my vision in the night I looked, and suddenly the four winds of heaven were churning up the great sea. Then four great beasts came up out of the sea, each one different from the others.” The first was like a lion with an eagle's wings, and Daniel watched until its wings were torn off and it was lifted up and made to stand on two feet like a man and given the mind of a man. The second was like a bear, raised up on one side, three ribs in its mouth between its teeth, and told, “Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!” The third was like a leopard, quick as the wind, with four wings of a bird on its back and four heads, “and it was given authority to rule.” Lions, bears, leopards: the statue of chapter 2 was made of metals stacked in order, but this time the empires arrive as animals, out of a churned sea, and each one is stranger and less governable than the one before.

The fourth beast broke the pattern of nature altogether. It was terrifying, “dreadful and extremely strong,” a thing “with large iron teeth. It devoured and crushed; then it trampled underfoot whatever was left,” and it had ten horns. While Daniel contemplated the horns, another came up among them, “a little one,” and three of the first horns were uprooted before it, and this horn “had eyes like those of a man and a mouth that spoke words of arrogance.” Iron has followed Daniel through this book, in legs and now in teeth, and here it stops being a building material and becomes an appetite. The vision's darkest figure so far is not the most powerful beast but the smallest horn on it, the one with human eyes and a talking mouth.

Then the camera of the vision lifts off the sea entirely. “As I continued to watch, thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of His head was like pure wool. His throne was flaming with fire, and its wheels were all ablaze. A river of fire was flowing, coming out from His presence. Thousands upon thousands attended Him, and myriads upon myriads stood before Him. The court was convened, and the books were opened.” The horn kept speaking its arrogant words somewhere below, but the vision no longer looks at it. The beast was slain in a single verse, its body destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire, while the other beasts were allowed an extension of life for a season, their dominion already removed. Judgment in this vision is not a battle. It is a session.

And into that court, out of the night sky, came the figure the whole book has been walking toward. “In my vision in the night I continued to watch, and I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence. And He was given dominion, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” Four beasts rose out of the sea and were given their seasons. One like a son of man came with the clouds and was given forever. Daniel does not explain him. He watches him approach the throne, and the episode closes with the court still in session and the interpretation still to come.

title: The Saints of the Most High
subtitle: Daniel 7
description: The interpretation: a horn at war with the saints, a court that convenes, and a kingdom given to a people.
paragraphs: “I, Daniel, was grieved in my spirit, and the visions in my mind alarmed me.” The dreamer does not celebrate his vision. He goes looking for one of the attendants standing in that fiery court and asks him “the true meaning of all this,” and the answer he receives is the shortest summary of the vision and the longest promise in the book: “These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth.” And then the promise: “the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever”, and, in the vision’s own emphasis, “yes, forever and ever.” Four kings from the earth, and then a people, not a fifth beast and not a fifth metal, receiving the kingdom at the end of the sequence. The statue dream had ended with a stone becoming a mountain. This one ends with the saints possessing the kingdom, and Daniel wanted to know more, especially about the fourth beast and its talking horn.

What he asks about is precise: the beast different from all the others, devouring and crushing with iron teeth and bronze claws; the ten horns; the other horn that rose and brought three down, “with eyes and with a mouth that spoke words of arrogance.” And then Daniel supplies the detail the first telling left in the shadows, what the horn was doing while it spoke: “As I watched, this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them, until the Ancient of Days arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High, and the time came for them to possess the kingdom.” Prevailing, the text says, and then until. The whole doctrine of the second half of Daniel stands in that until: the horn's success is real, and it is scheduled to end in a courtroom.

The interpretation of the fourth beast is given in the plainest terms the vision allows. “The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will appear on the earth, different from all the other kingdoms, and it will devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it.” The ten horns are ten kings from that kingdom, and after them another, different from the earlier ones, who subdues three kings. Then the vision names what this king is, not by his crown but by his mouth and his calendar: “He will speak out against the Most High and oppress the saints of the Most High, intending to change the appointed times and laws; and the saints will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.” The book does not name him here, any more than it named the statue's metals after the gold, and the telling leaves him as the text leaves him: a king known by his war on worship, on time, and on the saints.

Against that grant of time stands the court's sentence, in the vision's recurring grammar. “But the court will convene, and his dominion will be taken away and completely destroyed forever.” What follows is the transfer the whole chapter was built to reach: “Then the sovereignty, dominion, and greatness of the kingdoms under all of heaven will be given to the people, the saints of the Most High. His kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom, and all rulers will serve and obey Him.” The beasts came up out of the sea one by one and were each given a season. The kingdom given at the end is given to a people, and it is the only kingdom in either dream that is never taken back.

“Thus ends the matter.” Daniel's own postscript is the last word of the chapter and the most honest one in the book so far: “As for me, Daniel, my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face turned pale. But I kept the matter to myself.” He had asked for the true meaning and received it, and the meaning left him pale and silent. The prophet who explained kings' dreams to kings carried this one home unshared, and the book turns from his bedroom in Belshazzar's first year to another vision two years on, in the same reign, which he will need an angel to survive hearing explained.

title: The Ram, the Goat, and Gabriel
subtitle: Daniel 8
description: A ram, a goat flying without touching the ground, and Gabriel sent to explain the time of the end.
paragraphs: Two years after the beasts, in the third year of Belshazzar, Daniel saw a second vision, and this one begins with geography. “in the vision I saw myself in the citadel of Susa, in the province of Elam. I saw in the vision that I was beside the Ulai Canal.” He was in Babylon, and the vision set him in the Persian capital that did not rule the world yet, beside its river, watching animals again. A ram stood by the canal with two horns, both long, “but one was longer than the other, and the longer one grew up later,” and the ram charged west and north and south, and no animal could stand against him, and “there was no deliverance from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.”

Then out of the west came the challenger, “a goat with a prominent horn between his eyes,” moving at a speed the vision strains to draw: “crossing the surface of the entire earth without touching the ground.” The goat rushed at the ram “with furious power,” struck him, and shattered his two horns, threw him to the ground and trampled him, “and no one could deliver the ram from his power.” At the height of the goat's greatness the great horn broke, and “four prominent horns came up in its place, pointing toward the four winds of heaven.” Out of one of the four grew a little horn, and its growth was aimed: “toward the south and the east and toward the Beautiful Land,” up as high as the host of heaven, casting down stars and trampling them, magnifying itself “even to the Prince of the host,” removing His daily sacrifice and overthrowing “the place of His sanctuary.” The vision's arithmetic of violation is exact, because the next sound in it is a holy one asking another holy one how long. “It will take 2,300 evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be properly restored.”

Daniel was still turning the vision over when a voice from between the banks of the Ulai called a name the book has been waiting six chapters to hear: “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.” It is the first named angel in Daniel, sent not to shut lions' mouths but to teach, and Daniel's response to his approach was terror and a face in the dirt. Gabriel's first sentence sets the vision's address: “Son of man,” he said to me, “understand that the vision concerns the time of the end.” Daniel fell into a deep sleep where he stood, and the angel touched him and set him on his feet to hear the rest standing up.

The interpretation this time names its kingdoms outright, the only vision in the book that does. “The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia. The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece, and the large horn between his eyes is the first king.” The four horns are four kingdoms rising from that nation without its power. And in the latter part of their reign, Gabriel says, an insolent king will come, skilled in intrigue, whose power is great but not his own, who will destroy the mighty and the holy people, cause deceit to prosper, and “even stand against the Prince of princes. Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands.” The evenings and mornings spoken of are true, Gabriel closes, “Now you must seal up the vision, for it concerns the distant future.”

“I, Daniel, was exhausted and lay ill for days.” The vision's cost lands in the prophet's body, as it did after chapter 7's paleness, and when he rose he went back to the king's business with the seal still on what he had seen, and one sentence for his condition that every later reader of this chapter has recognized as their own: “I was confounded by the vision; it was beyond understanding.” He kept the interpretation he had been given. The understanding, Gabriel had already told him, belonged to a time of the end that was not his.

title: Daniel's Prayer
subtitle: Daniel 9
description: An old man reads Jeremiah's seventy years and answers with the longest confession in his book.
paragraphs: Babylon has fallen between chapters, and the book's most famous prayer begins with an old man reading. “In the first year of Darius son of Xerxes, a Mede by descent, who was made ruler over the kingdom of the Chaldeans”, Daniel writes, “in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years.” Daniel had been carried off as a boy in the first deportation, and Jeremiah's scroll, the prophet his generation left behind in Jerusalem, had promised the exile an end. Now the count was nearly run, a new empire sat on Babylon's throne, and the man who interpreted dreams for kings turned to a book and did the arithmetic of his own people's sentence. What the reading produced was not a claim. It was a confession: “So I turned my attention to the Lord God to seek Him by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.”

The prayer that follows is the longest sustained speech Daniel makes in his own book, and its grammar is all plural and all ownership. “O, Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant of loving devotion to those who love Him and keep His commandments, we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled. We have turned away from Your commandments and ordinances. We have not listened to Your servants the prophets, who spoke in Your name to our kings, leaders, fathers, and all the people of the land.” This is the man the administrators could find no negligence in, the innocent of the lions' den, confessing in the first person plural a rebellion he personally spent eighty years refusing. He does not pray as the exception to Israel. He prays as its representative, and the sins he names are not the ones committed in Babylon's palace but the ones Jeremiah catalogued in Jerusalem's streets.

The prayer's middle is a ledger of shame set against a single attribute of God. “To You, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but this day we are covered with shame,” shame for Judah, Jerusalem, and all Israel near and far, scattered “in all the countries to which You have driven us.” The curse of Moses' law has been poured out, exactly as written, and Daniel calls the catastrophe just while he is standing in its ruins: nothing done anywhere under heaven matches what was done to Jerusalem, “yet we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our iniquities and giving attention to Your truth. Therefore the LORD has kept the calamity in store and brought it upon us. For the LORD our God is righteous in all He does; yet we have not obeyed His voice.” Against that entire record he sets two words: “To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him.”

Only then does the prayer ask for anything, and what it asks for is not built on the asking. “So now, our God, hear the prayers and petitions of Your servant. For Your sake, O Lord, cause Your face to shine upon Your desolate sanctuary.” The plea is for Jerusalem's reproach to end because the city bears God's name, and Daniel says the ground of it out loud so no one can mistake the transaction: “For we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion.” The chapter's God has been righteous in every disaster and compassionate in every restraint, and the prayer leans its whole weight on the second of those.

It ends in a rush, three cries stacked like a man who has stopped composing and started calling out: “O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act! For Your sake, O my God, do not delay, because Your city and Your people bear Your name.” Daniel was still speaking, the next verse says, still confessing his sin and the sin of his people Israel, when the answer arrived faster than the prayer could finish. The man who had read a prophet's scroll and counted seventy years was about to be handed a new number entirely, seventy sevens, by the angel who had once been sent to explain a vision by a canal in Susa.

title: Seventy Sevens
subtitle: Daniel 9
description: Gabriel outruns the prayer and trades seventy years for seventy sevens, counted to a Messiah cut off.
paragraphs: The answer outran the prayer: “while I was still praying, Gabriel, the man I had seen in the earlier vision, came to me in swift flight about the time of the evening sacrifice.” The hour matters to the book: the evening sacrifice had not been offered in Jerusalem for decades, but Daniel's day still kept its time, and it was at that hour, mid-confession, that Gabriel arrived with a commission of his own. “O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding. At the beginning of your petitions, an answer went out, and I have come to tell you, for you are highly precious. So consider the message and understand the vision.” The confession that began by disclaiming all righteous acts is answered by a heaven that calls the confessor highly precious and dates its reply from the beginning of his petitions, before he had finished a sentence of them.

What Gabriel hands him is a number built on the number Daniel had just been reading. Daniel had counted seventy years in Jeremiah. The answer is seventy sevens. “Seventy weeks are decreed for your people and your holy city to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Most Holy Place.” Six purposes are listed, and they reach from the end of transgression to the anointing of the Most Holy Place, a larger errand than the one Daniel prayed about. He had asked for a desolate sanctuary to shine again. The answer describes the end of sin itself, measured out in sevens, and then divides the measure into its parts.

“Know and understand this: From the issuance of the decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the Messiah, the Prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress.” Seven sevens and sixty-two sevens are marked off toward an anointed prince, with the city rebuilt in trouble along the way, and then the sentence every generation of readers has slowed down for: “Then after the sixty-two weeks the Messiah will be cut off and will have nothing. Then the people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end will come like a flood, and until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed.” The anointed one is cut off, and after him the city and sanctuary whose rebuilding the count began with are destroyed a second time, by the people of a prince still to come.

The last seven is the most argued-over verse in the book. “And he will confirm a covenant with many for one week, but in the middle of the week he will put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of the temple will come the abomination that causes desolation, until the decreed destruction is poured out upon him.” A covenant confirmed and broken at its midpoint, sacrifice stopped, desolation set in the temple's wing, and a decreed end poured out on the desolator. The book gives Daniel the architecture of the seventy sevens and withholds the identifications his readers have sought in it ever since: which decree, which anointed one, which prince, whose week. Gabriel says consider the message and understand the vision, and then the chapter ends, and Daniel's prayer for his people's return has been answered with a calendar of the whole future, sealed not by its clarity but by its decrees.

The next time heaven speaks to Daniel at length, a decade and another empire will have passed, and he will be an old man fasting beside the Tigris in the third year of Cyrus, mourning three weeks over a message that “concerned a great conflict.” The seventy sevens stand behind him now, unexplained and unforgotten, and the book's final vision is about to open the long scroll of kings that leads from Persia's court to the end of days.

title: The Man by the Tigris
subtitle: Daniel 10
description: Three weeks of mourning by the Tigris, a man in linen, and a war in heaven that delayed the answer.
paragraphs: The book's last vision begins in grief with no named cause. “In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, a message was revealed to Daniel, who was called Belteshazzar. The message was true, and it concerned a great conflict.” Daniel mourned three full weeks, eating “no rich food,” letting no meat or wine enter his mouth, anointing himself with no oil, an old man past eighty by the book's arithmetic, fasting by a river in a land not his own, in the reign of the king who had let his people go home. Whatever he was mourning, the answer took the whole three weeks to reach him, and the chapter is careful to tell the reader why.

On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, standing on the bank of the Tigris, he lifted his eyes: “there was a certain man dressed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist. His body was like beryl, his face like the brilliance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of polished bronze, and his voice like the sound of a multitude.” Daniel alone saw it. The men with him saw nothing, “but a great terror fell upon them, and they ran and hid themselves,” and the prophet was left alone with the glory, drained: “No strength remained in me; my face grew deathly pale, and I was powerless.” He heard the sound of the man's words and fell into a deep sleep with his face to the ground, the posture he has taken before every great revelation since the Ulai Canal.

What raises him is touch, and then the sentence heaven has now said to him twice in this book: “Daniel, you are a man who is highly precious. Consider carefully the words that I am about to say to you. Stand up, for I have now been sent to you.” Trembling, he stood, and the messenger explained the three-week delay as a war the reader is permitted to overhear. “Do not be afraid, Daniel,” he said, “for from the first day that you purposed to understand and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I have come in response to them. However, the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed me for twenty-one days. Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, for I had been left there with the kings of Persia.” Twenty-one days of fasting on earth, twenty-one days of opposition in heaven, matched day for day. Daniel's words had been heard on the first day. The answer's road was the contested part.

The explanation of the delay undid him again. He set his face to the ground speechless, until one with the likeness of a man touched his lips and he could ask the question of every servant in the book's second half: “How can I, your servant, speak with you, my lord? Now I have no strength, nor is any breath left in me.” A second touch strengthened him, and the words that strengthened him were the chapter's whole errand in miniature: “Do not be afraid, you who are highly precious,” he said. “Peace be with you! Be strong now; be very strong!” Strengthened, Daniel said what the frightened boy at the Ulai could not have said: “Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me.”

Then the messenger names the war plainly and opens the book that the next two chapters will read aloud. He must return to fight the prince of Persia, and after him the prince of Greece will come. “But first I will tell you what is inscribed in the Book of Truth. Yet no one has the courage to support me against these, except Michael your prince.” Empires in this chapter have two faces at once, kings on the ground and princes contending above them, and one archangel assigned to Daniel's people stands against the sequence. The vision Daniel is about to receive, the longest in his book, arrives framed by that unseen war, and it begins with a voice telling an old man on a riverbank that everything he is about to hear is already written down somewhere.

title: Kings of the South and the North
subtitle: Daniel 11
description: The Book of Truth read aloud: kings of the South and North, a despicable king, and a sanctuary desecrated.
paragraphs: The reading from the Book of Truth opens in Persia. Three more kings will arise there, and then a fourth, “far richer than all the others,” who by his wealth will stir up everyone against Greece. Then a mighty king will arise, ruling with great authority and doing as he pleases, and “as soon as he is established, his kingdom will be broken up and parceled out toward the four winds of heaven,” not to his descendants, not with his authority, uprooted and given to others. The vision that spent three chapters on beasts and statues now runs at the speed of a chronicle, and it gives Daniel no names at all. It gives him directions: after the fourfold division settles, the rest of the chapter is a war between a king of the South and a king of the North, with the Beautiful Land lying on the road between them.

The wars run for generations in a handful of verses. The king of the South grows strong, and one of his commanders grows stronger and rules his own kingdom. An alliance is sealed with a royal marriage, the daughter of the South given to the North, and it fails: she loses her position, and is given up “along with her royal escort and her father and the one who supported her.” One from her family line rises and carries the war into the northern fortress and wins, hauling even the northern gods and their precious vessels down to Egypt as spoil. Sons stir up strife, armies sweep through like floods and are swept away, the South's king casts down tens of thousands in pride and does not triumph, the North returns with a larger army, builds a siege ramp, and takes a fortified city, and all the while the vision keeps its ledger of the Land: “The invader will do as he pleases, and no one will stand against him. He will establish himself in the Beautiful Land, with destruction in his hand.”

Midway through the wars the vision's tone changes, because a different kind of king enters the northern line. First comes one who sends out a tax collector “for the glory of the kingdom” and is destroyed within days, “though not in anger or in battle.” Then the vision says it plainly: “In his place a despicable person will arise; royal honors will not be given to him, but he will come in a time of peace and seize the kingdom by intrigue.” This king fights the South with plots as much as armies, sweeps away a flood of forces “along with a prince of the covenant,” enriches his followers with plunder his fathers never distributed, and turns his heart “against the holy covenant” on the road home. Checked once by the ships of Kittim, he turns back in rage on the covenant itself, and favors those who forsake it.

What he does in Jerusalem is the wound the whole vision has been approaching: “His forces will rise up and desecrate the temple fortress. They will abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation.” The daily sacrifice Daniel kept time by in Darius's reign, the one Gabriel interrupted at its evening hour, is abolished by a king the vision refuses to name. The response of God's people is given in one line, and it is the chapter's only portrait of them: “With flattery he will corrupt those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God will firmly resist him.” Some fall for it and some stand, and the standing ones teach: “Those with insight will instruct many, though for a time they will fall by sword or flame, or be captured or plundered.”

The episode ends inside the furnace of that resistance, on the vision's own explanation of what the suffering is for. “Now when they fall, they will be granted a little help, but many will join them insincerely. Some of the wise will fall so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless until the time of the end, for it will still come at the appointed time.” Refined, purified, made spotless: the vocabulary of the smelter, applied to people, with a deadline attached that is not theirs to set. The chapter does not end the wars here. Ahead of Daniel, still sealed in the same reading, stands one more king, who will do as he pleases and exalt himself above every god, and after him the end itself.

title: The King Who Exalts Himself, and the End of Days
subtitle: Daniel 11
description: A king who magnifies himself, Michael rising, the dead awakening, and Daniel promised his inheritance.
paragraphs: “Then the king will do as he pleases and will exalt and magnify himself above every god, and he will speak monstrous things against the God of gods.” The vision's last king is introduced without a compass point, no North or South attached, and his religion is himself: “He will show no regard for the gods of his fathers, nor for the one desired by women, nor for any other god, because he will magnify himself above them all.” In their place he honors “a god of fortresses,” a god his fathers did not know, paid in gold and silver and precious stones, and with that foreign god's help he attacks the strongest fortresses and sells the land to those who acknowledge him. He prospers, the vision says, “until the time of wrath is completed, for what has been decreed must be accomplished,” the same grammar as the little horn's career: real success, on a schedule, inside a decree.

At the time of the end the old geography reasserts itself one final time. The king of the South engages him, and the king of the North storms out “with chariots, horsemen, and many ships, invading many countries and sweeping through them like a flood.” He invades the Beautiful Land, and many countries fall, though Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites are delivered from his hand. Egypt does not escape; its treasures of gold and silver pass into his control, with Libyans and Cushites submitting after him. Then news from the east and north alarms him, and he goes out in great fury “to destroy many and devote them to destruction,” and pitches “his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain.” The sentence that ends him is the shortest royal obituary in the book: “but he will meet his end with no one to help him.” No battle is described. The man who magnified himself above every god dies unhelped between the sea and the mountain, and the vision moves on without a backward look.

Because what follows him is not another kingdom. “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands watch over your people, will rise up. There will be a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time.” But at that time, Daniel is told, your people, “everyone whose name is found written in the book”, will be delivered. And then chapter 12 speaks the sentence the whole Old Testament has been approaching: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt. Then the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.” Daniel is ordered to shut the words and seal the book until the time of the end, when many will roam to and fro and knowledge will increase. The kingdoms came up out of the sea and the dust. The last word about the dust is that it does not keep the wise.

The book closes as a conversation on the riverbank, and it closes with Daniel not understanding. Two others stand on the banks of the river, and one asks the man in linen above the waters how long until the fulfillment of these wonders, and the man raises both hands to heaven and swears by Him who lives forever: “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time. When the power of the holy people has finally been shattered, all these things will be completed.” Daniel says it plainly: “I heard, but I did not understand.” His last question in his own book is the reader's question, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?” and the answer refuses him the outcome and gives him a way to live instead: “Go on your way, Daniel,” he replied, “for the words are closed up and sealed until the time of the end.”

Numbers are given where understanding is not. From the abolishing of the daily sacrifice and the setting up of the abomination of desolation there will be 1,290 days, and “Blessed is he who waits and reaches the end of the 1,335 days.” And the final verse of the book is addressed to the old man himself, the boy carried to Babylon who outlived three empires and two of their kings' confessions, and it is the gentlest command Daniel ever received: “But as for you, go on your way until the end. You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.” The interpreter of everyone else's dreams is promised his own rising, in his own person, at the end of the days he spent his life being shown. The book shuts the words. It does not shut the promise.
